Vaja Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Vaja, Hungary

Not demolished. Jews first settled in Vaja in the early 19th century, numbering 20 by 1840 and peaking at 246 by 1910. The community, which affiliated Orthodox in 1876, maintained a synagogue, burial society, cheder, and mikveh, led by Jakab Rosenfeld rather than an employed rabbi. In April 1944, Vaja's Jews were confined in the synagogue for a full day - during which a local Baptist pastor brought them food and took their two Torah scrolls for safekeeping - before deportation to the Kisvárda Ghetto and then Auschwitz on Shavuot. Of 164 Jews present in 1944, 25 survivors returned to renovate the synagogue and clean the cemetery, but by 1960 only one Jewish family remained in Vaja. The cemetery's oldest tombstone dates to 1860, its newest to 1941.
